description: Mains AC and battery DC power, relays, motors, solenoids and output devices compared.
content_html:
Two Types of Electrical Power

Every electrical system needs a power supply. In engineering there are two fundamentally different types: alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).

UK mains electricity is 230 V AC at 50 Hz. The voltage swings between a positive peak and a negative peak 50 times per second, producing a smooth sine wave. If you display mains AC on an oscilloscope you see a repeating wave; if you display battery DC you see a flat horizontal line. Mains AC is used for high-power fixed equipment (motors, heaters, industrial machinery). Batteries produce DC and are used for portable, low-power and safety-critical applications.

Key Fact

Mains AC: 230 V, sine-wave waveform, high power, fixed location, not portable. Battery DC: typically 1.5–12 V, flat-line waveform, lower power, portable, finite energy store. Electronic circuits (microcontrollers, sensors, logic gates) require DC — a power supply unit (PSU) converts mains AC to regulated DC.

Transformers

A transformer changes the voltage of an AC supply. It consists of a primary coil (input) and a secondary coil (output) wound around a shared iron core. When AC flows in the primary coil, a changing magnetic field is created in the core; this induces a voltage in the secondary coil. Transformers only work with AC — a DC current creates a static magnetic field that induces nothing.

The relationship between voltages and number of turns is: $$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$ where \(V_p\) is primary voltage, \(V_s\) is secondary voltage, \(N_p\) is number of primary turns and \(N_s\) is number of secondary turns.

Example: a transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. If the primary is connected to 230 V AC: $$V_s = \frac{V_p \times N_s}{N_p} = \frac{230 \times 100}{2000} = 11.5\text{ V}$$ This is a step-down transformer (output lower than input), used to produce safe low-voltage DC from mains. Step-up transformers increase voltage (more secondary turns than primary) and are used in electricity grid transmission.

A rectifier converts AC into DC. A single diode produces half-wave rectification — it blocks every negative half-cycle, leaving only the positive pulses. A bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged in a diamond so that both the positive and negative half-cycles contribute to the output (full-wave rectification). The output is pulsing DC, which is smoothed by a capacitor to produce a steady DC voltage.

In practice, a mains-powered PSU contains a step-down transformer, a bridge rectifier and a smoothing capacitor — this chain produces the stable DC that electronic circuits need. Many also include a voltage-regulator IC to hold the output at an exact value (e.g. 5 V for a microcontroller).

Input Control Devices: Switches

A switch is the simplest input control device. Push-to-make switches (normally open) complete the circuit when pressed; push-to-break switches (normally closed) interrupt the circuit when pressed. Toggle switches, rotary switches and limit switches (triggered by a physical stop on a machine) are all common in engineering applications. Switches are direct inputs — they require a human or a mechanical actuator to operate them.

The Relay — Electrically Controlled Switch

A relay is an electromagnetic switch. A small current in the control coil creates a magnetic field that attracts an iron armature, closing (or opening) a separate set of contacts. The relay allows a low-voltage, low-current control signal (e.g. 5 V from a microcontroller) to switch a high-voltage, high-current circuit (e.g. 230 V AC motor). The two circuits are electrically isolated — a relay is the safe interface between control electronics and mains-powered equipment.

Key Fact

A relay uses a small control current to switch a large load current, and keeps the two circuits electrically isolated. This protects sensitive control electronics (microcontrollers, sensors) from the high voltages and currents of mains-powered output devices like motors and heaters.

Output devices convert electrical energy into other forms of energy. You need to know four types:

  • Electric motor — converts electrical energy into rotary mechanical energy. Used to drive pumps, conveyors, drills and fans. DC motors are common in battery-powered tools; AC motors power industrial machinery.
  • Solenoid — an electromagnet with a moveable iron core (plunger). When energised, the plunger is pulled into the coil, producing linear mechanical movement. Used in door locks, valve actuators and automatic dispensing machines. A solenoid converts electrical energy to linear mechanical motion.
  • Buzzer and bell — audible alarms that convert electrical energy to sound. A piezo buzzer uses a piezoelectric crystal that vibrates when current is applied. An electric bell uses an electromagnet and a striker on a spring.
  • Lamp (light) — converts electrical energy to light and heat. Indicator lamps (signal lights on control panels) and LED assemblies are output devices. LEDs are much more energy-efficient than filament lamps.

Choosing a Power Supply

The choice between mains and battery depends on four factors: power requirement, portability, safety and cost. A mains supply can deliver unlimited power continuously but requires fixed wiring and is dangerous if mishandled. Batteries are self-contained and portable but have a finite energy store and must be replaced or recharged. For safety reasons, all control electronics (sensors, microcontrollers, logic circuits) should operate at low DC voltages (typically 3.3–12 V) — mains AC must be stepped down and rectified before it can power them.
exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to explain AC vs DC, draw the waveform shape (sine wave for AC, flat horizontal line for DC) and describe the direction of current flow. Saying “AC changes direction” without mentioning the frequency (50 Hz in the UK) or the waveform shape will not earn full marks. For transformer calculations, write the formula \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\) first, then rearrange and substitute — show all working because method marks are available even if the arithmetic is wrong.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mains AC (230 V, 50 Hz, sine wave) powers fixed high-power equipment; battery DC (low voltage, flat-line) powers portable and control electronics — a transformer steps voltage up or down and a rectifier converts AC to DC.
  • The transformer equation \(V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s\) links voltages to turn counts; a step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns and is used to produce safe low-voltage DC from mains.
  • A relay uses a small control current to safely switch a large load current, electrically isolating the control circuit from the power circuit; output devices (motors, solenoids, buzzers, lamps) convert electrical energy to mechanical, sound or light energy.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes alternating current (AC)?
A) Current that flows continuously in one direction only
B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave
C) Current produced only by batteries
D) Current that is always at a fixed low voltage
practice_questions.marks: B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A step-down transformer has 3000 turns on the primary coil and is connected to a 230 V AC supply. The secondary coil has 150 turns.

Calculate the output voltage of the secondary coil.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns [1 mark]
Rearranged: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 150/3000 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= 11.5 V [1 mark for correct answer with unit]
[3 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using a battery power supply instead of a mains power supply in a portable engineering diagnostic tool.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct advantage, up to 2 marks:
- Batteries are portable — the tool can be used anywhere without needing a mains socket.
- Batteries produce DC directly, which electronic circuits require without additional conversion.
- Battery voltage is low (typically 3–12 V), making the device safer to handle than mains equipment.
- No mains cable required — the technician can move freely around a vehicle or machine.
[2 marks — vague answers like 'cheaper' or 'quicker' without context do not earn marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the function of a relay in an engineered system. Include in your answer:
(a) What the relay does
(b) Why electrical isolation between the two circuits is important
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
(a) A relay uses a small control current in an electromagnet/coil to attract an armature/switch contacts, which switches a separate circuit carrying a much larger current. [2 marks — 1 for 'small current controls large current', 1 for electromagnetic/physical mechanism]
(b) Isolation means the high-voltage/high-current power circuit (e.g. 230 V motor) is not electrically connected to the control circuit (e.g. 5 V microcontroller). This prevents high voltage damaging or destroying the sensitive control electronics. [2 marks — 1 for identifying the circuits as separate/not connected, 1 for consequence: protection of electronics]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a motor and a solenoid as output devices in an engineering system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A motor converts electrical energy into continuous rotary motion; a solenoid converts electrical energy into a single linear push or pull motion.
- Motors are used where sustained rotation is needed (e.g. pump, conveyor); solenoids are used where a short, controlled linear stroke is needed (e.g. door lock, valve).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Elwick Automation Ltd designs a control system for an automated chemical-dosing pump. The pump motor runs on 230 V AC mains. The control circuit uses a microcontroller operating at 5 V DC.

Evaluate the use of a relay to interface the microcontroller with the pump motor. In your answer, consider at least one alternative approach.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed explanation of the relay's function (small 5 V control signal drives coil, which switches the 230 V motor circuit). Evaluates advantages: electrical isolation protects the microcontroller from mains voltage, simple to implement, reliable, easily replaced. Evaluates disadvantages: relay switching is relatively slow (~10 ms), has moving parts that wear, produces a clicking noise. Considers an alternative (solid-state relay or TRIAC/thyristor): no moving parts, faster switching, silent, but more expensive and can fail silently without cutting power (safety concern in a chemical dosing context). Reaches a justified conclusion referencing the application.

Secure (5-6): Explains the isolation benefit clearly. Identifies at least one disadvantage and one alternative with some comparison. Conclusion present but may lack full engineering reasoning.

Developing (3-4): Describes relay function and one advantage. Limited alternative discussion.

Emerging (1-2): Basic relay description with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: UK mains electricity is 230 V AC. What does the 'AC' mean?
options: The current flows in one direction only
The current reverses direction 50 times per second
The current is produced by a battery

knowledge_checks.q: What is the primary purpose of a relay in a control circuit?
options: To use a small control current to switch a large load current, with electrical isolation
To measure current in a circuit

knowledge_checks.q: A transformer that has more secondary turns than primary turns is called a step-_____ transformer and increases the output voltage.
A solenoid converts electrical energy into _____ mechanical motion.
Match each output device to the energy conversion it performs:
right: Electrical energy to rotary mechanical energy
Electrical energy to linear mechanical motion

flashcard_questions.q: What waveform does mains AC produce on an oscilloscope?
What waveform does battery DC produce on an oscilloscope?
What is the UK mains voltage and frequency?

flashcard_questions.a: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns (primary voltage over secondary voltage equals primary turns over secondary turns).
A transformer with fewer secondary turns than primary turns, producing a lower output voltage.
Converts AC to DC by allowing current to flow in one direction only, using diodes.
An electromagnetic switch that uses a small control current to switch a circuit carrying a much larger current.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is electrical isolation in a relay important?
flashcard_questions.a: It prevents high voltage in the load circuit from damaging sensitive control electronics.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an electric motor convert electrical energy into?
What does a solenoid produce when energised?
flashcard_questions.a: A linear push or pull movement of its metal plunger.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four main output devices in an electrical system.
Why do electronic circuits need DC rather than AC?
flashcard_questions.a: Electronic components (microcontrollers, logic gates) require a constant-direction current at a stable low voltage.

glossary_terms.definition: Electricity in which the direction of current flow reverses many times per second, forming a sine wave. UK mains is 230 V AC at 50 Hz.
Electricity that flows continuously in one direction only. Batteries and power-supply units (PSUs) produce DC.
An electromagnetic device that steps AC voltage up or down using two coils (primary and secondary) wound on a shared iron core.
A circuit that converts AC into DC by allowing current to flow in one direction only, using diodes.
A component that manually or automatically makes or breaks an electrical circuit.
An electromagnetic switch that uses a small control current to open or close a circuit carrying a much larger current.
An output device that uses an electromagnet to produce a linear push or pull movement of a metal plunger.
